title: Catch Your Breath: Adaptive Computation for Self-Paced Sequence Production
claim: A model can signal uncertainty to trigger extra compute steps per token, yielding adaptive, variable computation across a sequence.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; schematic transformer left, heatmapped text right
description: Panel (a) is a schematic of a transformer unrolled over five positions. Each position is a column with an input box at the bottom, two gray layer blocks stacked above it, and a colored output box at the top. An 'activation' arrow points upward on the left. Curved arrows labeled "don't know" link outputs from one column to the next. Those links cause the next inputs to be white boxes labeled 'pause'. Panel (b) shows a paragraph of real-estate text about a neighborhood. Each token is shaded in blue, from light to dark, to show how many compute steps it received. A legend above runs from 1 step to 4 steps. The dark highlights on some tokens, such as the first word and certain names and numbers, show that the model spends more compute on harder tokens.
caption: (a) Sequence processing in a transformer with <don’t know> outputs that trigger <pause> inputs. (b) The CYB loss yields variable per-token computing steps. When the <don’t know> probability is high, additional computing steps are provided. Shading indicates the expected number of computing steps to predict the corresponding token. Spacing reflects token boundaries.
abstract: Within the landscape of inference-time scaling methods for foundation models, a width-based approach to scaling--which involves the insertion of <pause> tokens in the input stream to delay model responses--offers a unique advantage by increasing model expressivity while remaining highly parallelizable at both training and inference. The existing literature on training models to utilize <pause> tokens relies on the standard cross-entropy objective in which the model output is read out and evaluated only at the final step of a pause sequence. This approach provides no mechanism for the model to regulate its own processing or to signal readiness to respond, treating the additional compute steps as a barrier to skip over rather than a resource to be used adaptively. We propose a supervised loss, Catch Your Breath (CYB), framed as a sequential-decision problem, that trains a model to dynamically and autonomously scale the number of compute steps used for each input token. The model indicates the need for additional compute steps by emitting a special <don't know> output, delaying its response via a pause. The model can abstain multiple times to obtain longer delays. Our experiments demonstrate that when <pause> tokens are included in the input stream, pretraining or fine-tuning with CYB significantly outperforms standard cross-entropy, reducing perplexity and enhancing downstream accuracy with no additional computational or memory cost.
